item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] I left Gaza, but my body is trapped in the horrors of war
item.description:
I left Gaza, but my body is trapped in the horrors of war

Submitted by Reem Salim on Fri, 10/02/2026 - 15:00
Ordinary sounds like the call to prayer, or the sight of an airplane overhead, still leave me tense and fearful
Smoke and fire rise after an Israeli air strike on a house in Khan Younis, in the southern Gaza Strip, on 9 September 2026 (Bashar Taleb/AFP)
On

I left Gaza on 19 February 2024, but sometimes, it feels as though I am still trapped there.

While I physically survived the war, its ghosts still haunt me through the memories spurred by certain sights and sounds, and in how my body involuntarily reacts.

In Egypt today, the call to prayer, which is supposed to bring peace to my soul, leaves me tense and terrified. My heart races and I struggle to breathe, fearing that death is imminent.

In October 2023, I was sitting with my family watching the news as the adhan from a nearby mosque minaret filled the air. Suddenly, I felt my body being thrown violently, as I choked on the smell of gunpowder. An intense Israeli bombardment had struck our neighbour’s house. 

A large piece of stone shattered the window a few centimetres from me. I gasped out the words of the shahada, believing I was about to die. 

To this day, every time the call to prayer reaches my ears, it takes me back to that moment.

The war also triggered my fear of airplanes. When a plane flies over the skies of Egypt, I do not imagine an ordinary aircraft carrying passengers, but rather a fighter jet carrying missiles that could fall on us at any moment.

Permanent damage

These are not the only things that affect me. On one hand, I can still see the scars left by stitches around my middle finger, which looks different from the others; the nail no longer grows normally.

It happened after we were displaced to my grandmother’s house in Deir al-Balah, amid repeated attacks on our own neighbourhood. Her house was crowded with other displaced people, and I was sitting in the dark one day when a missile exploded nearby. 

I feared that my younger brother, who could hear with only one ear, would lose his hearing in the other one from the force of the explosion - so I rushed towards him after hearing him cry, and told him to go to my mother. 

War on Gaza: Our memories of home will never die
Read More »

That was when another displaced child in the room, surely terrified by all that was happening around us, slammed the door in front of me, catching my finger between the door and its frame. The force severed the tip of my finger, tearing off my nail. At Al-Aqsa Martyrs Hospital, my finger was stitched without anesthesia, as I cried from the severe pain.

The wound healed, but the injury brought a new phobia: a fear of doors. Today, when I see someone place their hands near the side of a doorframe, my heart tightens and I grow tense.

Beyond my memory and senses, the war took over part of my body, too. Sometimes, all it takes is for me to sit down to feel it.

I was diagnosed with chronic inflammation in my tailbone as a result of sitting for long periods on a hard surface. The conditions of displacement forced me to sit on the floor all the time. I felt terrible pain, but hoped it was temporary and would disappear with time, planning to make an appointment with a specialist when the war ended. 

Instead, the pain became a permanent companion. One doctor in Egypt told me there was no option but to undergo surgery to remove the coccyx, which would itself have serious consequences - so I’ve learned to live with the pain.

People say that time heals everything, but three years on, I have come to realise that the body has a memory that cannot be erased. It will continue to respond to certain sounds and scenes as though danger is still present. 

How can I say that I survived the war, when my body is still trapped in its horrors to this day?

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] After Colombia's exit, what is left of the Hague Group?
item.description:
After Colombia's exit, what is left of the Hague Group?

Submitted by Ana Maria Monjardino on Mon, 10/05/2026 - 14:36
Three founding members have quit the coalition since March, while South Africa faces accusations of 'hypocrisy' over coal shipments to Israel
In this file photo, state representatives from South Africa and Colombia chair the opening conference of The Hague Group summit in Bogota, 15 July 2025 (Progressive International)
Off

Under former president Gustavo Petro, the Colombian state found it so difficult to halt coal shipments to Israel through diplomatic and bureaucratic channels that Petro called on the Wayuu, an Indigenous people of La Guajira, to occupy the train lines.

Now, his right-wing successor has signed a decree resuming those exports, and Colombia has walked away from the Hague Group, the coalition it once co-chaired to hold Israel to account for breaches of international law.

Its departure in August made it the third founding member, alongside Bolivia and Honduras, to leave the Hague Group in six months, leaving co-chair South Africa to steer the bloc alone.

The Hague Group was founded in January 2025 by these nations, joined also by Cuba, Malaysia, Namibia and Senegal.

"The Hague Group was born to advance international law in an era of impunity," South African Minister of International Relations Ronald Lamola told the meeting.

“Not only for the people of Gaza but for the future of a world where justice prevails over impunity,” the group agreed to take “coordinated legal and diplomatic measures” against Israel’s genocide in the midst of international failure to stop the carnage and complicity in Israel’s actions. 

This month, at the 81st session of the UN General Assembly, 40 countries gathered to address how states can act collectively to ensure that international law is not merely proclaimed, but enforced.

“It is also important to understand that The Hague Group is not a body that drafts, consolidates or passes new norms of international law,” explained Guillaume Long, diplomatic advisor to the Hague Group. Instead, it provides “a platform for states to try and articulate strategies, coordinate measures and have discussions,” he told Middle East Eye. However, he added, “the application of international law is usually at the domestic level.” 

The group is a kind of coalition of the willing attempting to ensure that international law is enforced in the face of a push by the United States and its allies to dismantle much of the global legal and humanitarian order.

Political will is therefore essential. But in Latin America, a region where pink-wave politics once galvanised government support for Palestinians rights, the rise of a new right-wing order has led to the withdrawal of three founding Hague Group members.

Meanwhile, as bombs continue falling on Gaza, ethnic cleansing escalates in the West Bank and the rule of law is under escalating threat from Palestine to Cuba, The Hague Group faces an up-hill battle. 

Losing Latin America

In March, founding members Honduras and Bolivia promptly withdrew following the respective presidential victories of Nasry Asfura and Rodrigo Paz. Asfura, in particular, ramped up relations and extended a warm welcome to Israeli leaders, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, wanted for crimes against humanity by the International Criminal Court (ICC), before even entering office. 

Co-chair Colombia also withdrew in August, following the election as president of right-wing populist Abelardo de la Espriella. 

After less than two months in office, De La Espriella has appointed a new ambassador, recognised Israel's claim over the illegally occupied Golan Heights, abolished visa requirements for Israelis, restored the Colombia-Israel Free Trade Agreement, and withdrawn from South Africa's case against Israel at the International Court of Justice (ICJ). 

'We are seeing Colombia deliver on what it offered: to boycott, sabotage, withdraw from multilateralism, and abandon its cause for Palestinian self-determination'

- Guillaume Long, diplomatic adviser to The Hague Group

But one of Petro’s former diplomats says the reversal is not simply a matter of presidential prerogative but may put Colombia in breach of its legal obligations. 

“The Colombian government has international obligations and is bound by international law,” said Mauricio Jaramillo Jassir, former deputy foreign minister of Colombia under Petro.

“So while the constitution grants the president the authority and capacity to conduct diplomacy, that diplomacy must be managed within the framework of international law,” he told Middle East Eye, pointing to the binding legal obligation of third-party states to prevent and punish genocide under the 1948 Genocide Convention. 

Colombia also withdrew the long-standing nomination of Colombian lawyer and former ambassador to the Netherlands, Carolina Olarte-Bacares, who co-led Colombia’s delegation in support of South Africa’s ICJ case against Israel, for an ICC judgeship.

This leaves Latin America and the Caribbean without the possibility of representation despite representing 8.2 percent of the world’s population. 

“We are seeing Colombia deliver on what it offered: to boycott, sabotage, withdraw from multilateralism, and of course abandon its cause for Palestinian self-determination,” said Long. 

De La Espriella is following in the footsteps of US President Donald Trump who, alongside Secretary of State Marco Rubio, is ramping up efforts to dismantle the ICC, in part an effort to buttress Israeli impunity. Doubling down during his UN General Assembly address this month, Trump called on members to resign from the “evil” and “rogue” institution. 

This onslaught against international institutions is not without opposition among the majority of UN member states, Long tells MEE, insisting that “there is a growing consensus that these attacks to destroy the institutions of international justice are completely outrageous”.

'Hypocrisy' at the ports 

At the BRICS summit in Delhi on 12 September, in a speech focused on inclusive global governance and strengthening the multinational system, South African President Cyril Ramaphosa called for "comprehensive Security Council reform”. He pointed to the importance of accountability for atrocities, including “for the genocide committed against the people of Palestine”. 

Alongside accountability, implementation was central to the agenda of the meeting at the UN General Assembly this month.

“The measures adopted in Bogota show that we are serious and that coordinated state action is possible,” announced Lamola at the summit, referring to an emergency meeting held in July 2025. Agreed upon by 13 states, those measures included a pledge to prevent the provision, transfer and transit of arms and dual-use items to Israel.

And yet, in August 2025, after Petro issued a presidential decree banning coal exports to Israel, South Africa stepped in, allowing the Anglo-Swiss mining giant Glencore, which had supplied Colombian coal to Israel for decades, to relocate its core operations. 

Malaysia seizes container suspected of carrying goods bound for Israel
Read More »

Although the state does not mine or sell the coal itself, “it exercises decisive regulatory authority over whether such exports may lawfully occur,” a report by BDS South Africa said. It added that this is a “direct contradiction” to South Africa’s Hague Group commitments and as a result “South Africa is fuelling the ongoing genocide”.

“The South African government talks ‘left’ by going to The Hague and walks ‘right’ by ignoring the sources of profit and trade,” said Patrick Bond, director of the Centre for Social Change at the University of Johannesburg. The export of coal bound for Israel from Richards Bay on South Africa's northeast coast “is the most extreme form of hypocrisy,” he explained. 

Bond previously told MEE that Ramaphosa’s government has every capacity to end coal exports to Israel through a category called dangerous exports. “The coal could be switched off immediately,” he said at the time. But the ruling elite of South Africa, including President Ramaphosa himself, has close ties to the extractive industry. 

In 2014, in order to assume the deputy presidency under Jacob Zuma, Ramaphosa was forced to divest his mining interests, including ownership of the Glencore-allied firm Shanduka, and his role as a local chairperson on the board of Optimum Coal, in which Glencore had a controlling interest. 

To this day, his brother-in-law, Patrice Motsepe, is the founder and non-executive chairman of African Rainbow Minerals (ARM) which operates ARM Coal in partnership with Glencore. As a result, ARM Coal holds access to Glencore’s “interest and entitlement” in Richards Bay. 

In contrast to South Africa's failure to halt coal exports, on 8 August, the Malaysian Border Control and Protection Agency (AKPS) seized a container of suspected strategic trade cargo intended for export to Israel at the Port of Tanjung Pelepas.

“This action demonstrates Malaysia's firm stance to ensure that our country will never serve as a conduit for trade that could support or contribute to the Israeli regime's atrocities against the Palestinian people,” said Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim. “It is also in line with Malaysia's commitments under The Hague Group.” 

One week later, Malaysian authorities seized several more Israel-bound shipments. 

"It is because of the fact that states are not all in compliance with their third-state obligations that The Hague Group was created,” explained Long. “Our role in The Hague Group, regardless of what we may think or what we may personally consider to be the right course of action, is to try and consolidate coordinated state action,” he told MEE. 

The Hague Group is “a complex panorama of states that have done things with complex repercussions on the politics of their countries,” said Long. South Africa, for example, lost substantial US aid after launching its ICJ case against Israel. Likewise, Colombia’s Petro had his US visa revoked after calling for an armed front to directly oppose Israel’s genocide. 

Civil society 

Moving forward, “the future lies in understanding that foreign policy is not the exclusive monopoly of the government,” said Colombia's Jaramillo Jassir. “I see this as an opportunity for the group to adapt and work more closely with civil society and social organisations,” he told MEE.

“The challenge lies in making membership more flexible, establishing channels with civil society, and expanding to include other governments to gain broader representation,” he explained. 

Colombia stopped energy exports to Israel - so why did South Africa and Brazil not do so?
Read More »

In Colombia, the NGO group Resist Glencore has been at the forefront of civil society organising against the transfer of coal to Israel, which constituted 51 percent of Israel’s thermal coal supply until August 2024. It works in solidarity with the Wayuu and the Yukpa, indigenous communities heavily impacted by operations at Glencore’s massive open-pit mining complex in La Guajira, El Cerrejon. 

During the Petro administration, this included pushing for a second and more exacting decree to ban thermal coal exports “without exception” due to loopholes in the original. And the impact was tangible, with Colombian supplies to Israel plummeting from 34 percent after the first decree to six percent after the second. 

The decree’s quantifiable success indicates that the implementation of international law necessitates both political will and civil society pressure. “It was massively facilitated by the fact that we had a pro-Palestine government but it was also thanks to the work of social movements,” explained a representative from Resist Glencore.

In fact, “it was so difficult [for Petro] to proceed in a diplomatic, bureaucratic way, that he called for the Wayuu to occupy the train lines,” said the representative, who requested anonymity for reasons of security. 

In contrast, De la Espriella has promised to expand extractive mining and apply a militarised approach to combating crime. This has created a climate of fear for indigenous communities and trade union leaders who have historically borne the brunt of these tactics. Weeks after entering office, he also signed a decree to resume coal exports to Israel.  

Resist Glencore is currently working with former ministers from Petro’s government to push for a bill for an energy embargo in the Colombian Congress, where Petro's Historic Pact is the largest group.

The coal being used to power Israel’s genocide in Palestine is also destroying the local environment and leading to disproportionate child mortality at the point of extraction, the representative explained. 

From Gaza to La Guajira, “these things are completely connected,” they said.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Israel’s embrace of Serb nationalist Milorad Dodik threatens Bosnia and the wider Balkans
item.description:
Israel’s embrace of Serb nationalist Milorad Dodik threatens Bosnia and the wider Balkans

Submitted by Elis Gjevori on Wed, 10/07/2026 - 15:39
Israel’s growing ties with Republika Srpska embolden Dodik and give the entity another means of applying pressure on Europe
Former president Milorad Dodik of Republic of Srpska and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu meeting on 28 January (X/Screenshot)
Off

Pro-Israeli Serbian nationalist Milorad Dodik's bloc has emerged as a winner of Bosnia’s weekend elections.

His ally Zeljka Cvijanovic, of the right-wing Alliance of Independent Social Democrats (SNSD), secured more than 55 percent of the Serbian vote to retain a seat on Bosnia’s three-member presidency, which is divided between Bosniak Muslims, Croats and Serbs.

Israel’s Foreign Minister Gideon Saar inflamed tensions within the state with his endorsement of the separatist figure.

Dodik, the former president of the country’s Serb-majority entity, Republika Srpska, received a political ban in 2025 after challenging the authority of Bosnia's former international peace envoy Christian Schmidt.

Saar congratulated “President Dodik” and Cvijanovic in a statement on X.

“This is a strong vote of confidence for Republika Srpska and President Dodik's leadership and policies,” added Saar, without mentioning Bosnia and Herzegovina in that message.

He separately congratulated the Croat member of the presidency but issued no corresponding message to the Bosniak Muslim member.

In January, Dodik said he had asked Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to help Republika Srpska re-establish its "army, finances, courts, intelligence services".

The request is one of the clearest articulated threats to Bosnia's internationally recoginsed borders. 

'You will have to recognise Srebrenica genocide'

Bosnians voted on Sunday for three presidency members representing Bosniaks, Croats and Serbs under the country’s complex multi-ethnic system.

Voters also elected state and entity legislatures and the president of Republika Srpska.

Bosnia comprises two entities: the Muslim-majority Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Republika Srpska, which ethnic Serbs dominate after the genocide and ethnic cleansing of the 1990s war.

Bosnian philosopher and sociologist Professor Asim Mujkic told Middle East Eye that Bosnia’s constitutional framework “encourages ethnic political organisation to the detriment of other forms”.

“Such a fragmented electoral system,” said Mujkic, “can only deepen divisions and lead straight to an autocratic, not democratic, form of the government of which Dodik is an excellent example.”

Dodik, who has visited Israel at least three times this year alone, wants Republika Srpska to secede from Bosnia and join Serbia. He has found a receptive audience in Israel, which was established after the ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in 1948 and has been conducting its own genocide in Gaza since 2023.

'Such a fragmented electoral system ... can only deepen divisions and lead straight to an autocratic, not democratic, form of the government of which Dodik is an excellent example'

- Professor Asim Mujkic

Dodik denies the Srebrenica genocide.

The political philosophy of leaders such as Dodik, said Mujkic, “is rooted in general unwillingness of Serb political and intellectual classes to confront the past and crimes committed in their name”.

“This blackmail's narrative goes like this: if you don't vote for me, if you don't support my politics Serbs will be declared genocidal people, Republika Srpska or Serbia will be abolished as genocidal entities, you will have to recognise genocide in Srebrenica and independence of Kosovo,” said Mujkic.

Dodik’s outreach offers Israeli leaders, the journalists who interview him, and the wider public a kindred spirit who seems to understand their sense of grievance.

Israel has already demonstrated its willingness to back breakaway territories, recognising Somaliland in December 2025.

In a fawning September piece, the Jerusalem Post asked Dodik whether he thought about breaking up Bosnia and joining Serbia.

“Do I think about it?” Dodik said. “I dream about it. Absolutely,” he added. 

In a sign that Israel is deepening its presence in Bosnia, in September it opened an Israeli Chamber of Commerce office in Banja Luka, the seat of Republika Srpska.

Israel 'exploiting ethnic conflicts'

Denijal Jegic, an assistant professor of communication, told MEE that the “increase in cooperation between both entities appears primarily important for propaganda purposes”.

“Both entities are internationally rather isolated; backing from the Israeli regime can be beneficial not only for Dodik’s separatist goals but also for his aspiration of closer ties with the United States,” added Jegic.

For Dodik, the prospects of breaking away have arguably never looked more favourable.

Israeli influence within the Trump administration, alongside Donald Trump’s appetite for unconventional deals, creates an opening for Dodik to push his separatist ambitions more aggressively.

'The [Israeli] regime has long tried to exploit ethnic conflicts for its own benefit, seeking alliances with smaller entities, in which Israel maintains a position of hegemony'

- Assistant professor Denijal Jegic

“The Israeli attempts to empower the separatist tendencies of the Republika Srpska entity are surely a further threat to the already fragile sovereignty of Bosnia and Herzegovina because they can be presented as a form of outside legitimacy to the secession of the Republika Srpska entity,” warned Jegic.

For Israel, empowering Dodik also offers a bargaining chip against Europe.

As European governments take tentative steps towards holding Israel accountable for the genocide in Gaza, its support for Dodik sends a threatening message: Israel can help destabilise the Balkans, exposing Europe to another crisis.

The danger is a return to the bloodshed of the 1990s, with Bosniaks, Albanians and Serbs again paying the price. Europe would confront that threat while supporting Ukraine against Russia’s invasion.

Jegic said Israel’s growing influence in the Balkans had largely piggybacked on the United States, the European Union and Nato, which are also “the main backers of the Israeli regime”, he said.

“But precisely these circumstances may have helped Israel advance its influence in the region which now appears more important due the international isolation the regime has faced,” said Jegic.

“The [Israeli] regime has long tried to exploit ethnic conflicts for its own benefit, seeking alliances with smaller entities, in which Israel maintains a position of hegemony,” added Jegic.
